subtype: Approach: designs a team project by listing how it would fall apart [Action]
passage: I'm Rajni, and I sat behind Lokesh's team in the design lab while they planned their final-year project. Instead of dividing up tasks, Lokesh asked the group, 'How could we make this project fall apart?' They wrote answers on the board: nobody knows who is doing what, everything gets merged the night before, and one of us can't be reached when needed. Then, quickly, they answered each one. A role for each person on a sheet. A merge every Friday, not at the end. And one page of everyone's contact numbers, two each. Lokesh photographed the board. I can't say whether they were excited or just efficient, but at the demo, when one member fell ill, someone else already knew that part.

qa.q: On which day of the week did the team plan to merge?
qa.a: They planned to merge every Friday.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been feeling when asking how the project could fall apart?
qa.a: Lokesh was perhaps cautious and wanted to head off trouble, though Rajni can't be sure of the inner state.

qa.q: What other step could the team add to keep everyone in touch?
qa.a: The team could send a short message each evening saying what each person did, since it shows early when someone is stuck.

qa.q: How might the member who fell ill have felt when someone already knew that part?
qa.a: That member was probably relieved, since the work could go on without them.

grounding: Shows a student team listing how their project could fall apart and setting roles, weekly merges and a shared contact sheet.

subtype: Approach: designs a team project by listing how it would fall apart [Action]
passage:
Monday. The group project on city water supply was due in five weeks, and last semester's group had fallen apart. Deepika opened the first meeting with a strange question. "How would we wreck this project? Be honest."
Harsha laughed, then answered. "Nobody knows who's doing what. We merge everything the night before. Someone stops replying."
Deepika wrote each one on the whiteboard and then turned each into a rule. Roles by name, today. Merge every Friday. A shared sheet with everyone's number and a backup email.
Friday, two weeks later. The weekly merge showed Harsha's section clashed with the map data. They fixed it in forty minutes instead of finding it at midnight.
Submission day. When one member went home for a family function and stopped answering, Deepika called the backup number from the sheet and got the final chart by noon.

qa.q: How often did the team merge their work?
How might Harsha have felt when the weekly merge caught the clash early?
qa.a: Harsha was probably relieved, since fixing it in forty minutes was far better than finding it at midnight.

qa.q: What else could the group add to its rules, and why?
qa.a: They could agree a date for a full practice read of the report, so problems in flow or style show up before the final week.

qa.q: How might the member who went home for the family function see the backup number being used?
qa.a: That member may feel a bit embarrassed about going quiet but grateful that the sheet made it easy to still send the chart.

grounding: It shows a student team listing what would spoil their project, then setting named roles, weekly merges and a shared contact sheet.

subtype: Approach: designs a team project by listing how it would fall apart [Action]
passage:
Anirban, you're starting your final-year project, so let your Akash Dada tell you how ours nearly didn't happen.
Four of us, a bridge design model, three months. First meeting, our guide asked, "How could this project fail completely?" We thought it was a trick question.
Then we started. One: nobody knows whose job the calculations are. Two: all our files come together on the last day and nothing fits. Three: Rohan goes home to Siliguri and his phone doesn't work there.
Our guide said, "Good. Now fix each."
So we wrote names next to jobs. Every Saturday we combined files, even if half-done. And we made a sheet with every phone number, home landline and email.
Guess what. In week ten, Rohan did go home, and the sheet had his home number. That saved our model, beta.

qa.q: Where did Rohan go home to?
What did Akash and the team feel when the guide asked how the project could fail?
qa.a: They felt puzzled and a little suspicious, thinking it was a trick question.

qa.q: At the first meeting, what could the team have done instead, and how might it have gone?
qa.a: They could have skipped the question and just started building, but then the week-ten absence would likely have left them without Rohan's part.

qa.q: How might Rohan have been affected by the contact sheet?
qa.a: Rohan could still be reached at home in week ten, so he stayed part of the project instead of feeling he had let everyone down.

grounding: It shows a student team listing how their project would fall apart and setting named roles, weekly merges and a shared contact sheet.
